newsitem.title: MEXICO: TMM seen hurt by weak Far East business.
newsitem.headline: TMM seen hurt by weak Far East business.

text.p: Mexican transport giant Transportacion Maritima Mexicana (TMM) posted disappointing results on low demand in the Far East in 1996, analysts said on Wednesday.

TMM's operating margins shrank in part on a regional slump that affected all transportation companies. But TMM, which does one-third of its business in the Far East, was particularly hard hit, posting a 0.5 percent decline in trade and a six percent overcapacity in the region, analysts said.
"At the operating income level the results were the worst we have seen since we began following the company," Bear Stearns analyst Santiago Pique wrote in a report Wednesday.
He estimated the company's 1997 first- and second-quarter results will also be weak because of expected continuing low demand in the Far East.

Phokion Potamianos, an analyst with Caspian Securities in New York, estimated the company likely will continue reporting lower returns on equity in 1997. A more competitive Latin American market is attracting more companies to the market that TMM once dominated, he added.

Despite greater revenues and volumes in the liner business, rail, trucking and port operations, a weak Far East market dragged consolidated margins to an all-time low of 0.3 percent for the fourth quarter and 5.6 percent for the year, compared to 8.3 percent and 8.9 percent, respectively, in 1995.
In a recent conference call, the company proposed redesigning its Far East routes to target more profitable markets and replacing larger ships in the region with smaller, faster ones, analysts said.
The cost will be funded from $15 million set aside to restructure the route and return it to profitability by the second half of 1997, Bear Stearns's Pique said.
TMM said it plans capital expenditures of $67 million in 1997, not including the $306 million for its railroad venture Transportacion Ferroviaria Mexicana (TFM), according to Pique.
